questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify progress claimed without comparable measurement
questions.stem: A survey team reports that the wetland is in better condition than a decade ago, because plant cover looks thicker from the path.

options.text: A view from the path cannot show that the condition improved over a decade
Thicker cover on the path is enough to confirm recovery across the whole wetland
options.misconception: extrapolates a single vantage point to the whole site

options.text: The wetland must have improved, because the path itself has become clearer
options.misconception: reads clearer access as ecological recovery

options.text: Recovery cannot be shown without a full species inventory of the wetland
options.misconception: sets an unreasonably high bar for any finding

questions.explanation: Progress has to be demonstrated by comparable measurements across time, and a single view from the path supplies neither a baseline nor a sample. The alternatives either overreach from one vantage point or demand more than the claim requires.
questions.hint: Ask what was measured, and against what baseline.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Judge a period boundary against the evidence behind it
questions.stem: A regional bird atlas divides its record into a pre-farming phase and a farming phase, and the second phase covers three centuries.

options.text: The division is objective, since farming really began at that date
options.misconception: treats a chosen boundary as a discovered date

options.text: A second period is unnecessary, so the atlas should cover one continuous span
options.misconception: refuses periodization because it is a choice

options.text: The division is defensible because the farming period has its own evidence
Period lengths should be equal, so the atlas must split the record in two
options.misconception: judges periodization by symmetry rather than evidence

questions.explanation: Periodization is a choice the writer must defend with evidence about the period being claimed, and its length does not decide its validity. A three-century farming phase is as legitimate as a shorter one if the record supports it.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence marks the start of the second period.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a shared input from a shared cause
questions.stem: Two valleys far apart show the same decline in pollinator visits to the same crop, and both valley floors were planted with the same herbicide-resistant seed.

options.text: The seed choice explains the declines, since both valleys used the same variety
options.misconception: credits a shared input without checking shared local causes

options.text: Both valleys share the seed, but each valley may have its own local driver
A single driver must explain both declines, since the effect is identical everywhere
options.misconception: assumes matching effects must have matching causes

options.text: The declines cannot be compared, because the two valleys are far apart
options.misconception: dismisses a comparison because the sites differ

questions.explanation: Two sites sharing an input and an outcome is a reason to consider both, not to assume one cause. Local conditions may differ so much that the shared seed is a shared condition rather than a shared cause.
questions.hint: Ask what is different between the two valleys.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to test whether an outcome depended on an intervention
questions.stem: Explain to a survey team how to test whether a population's recovery was contingent on a particular intervention.

answer.exemplar: Contingency means the outcome would not have followed without the intervention, so a test must compare what happened with the intervention against what would have happened without it. For a recovering population, that means either a site that received no treatment, or a before-and-after record combined with evidence that the recovery did not already begin. Where no comparison exists, the team can look for a dose or intensity relationship, since a stronger response where the treatment was stronger supports contingency, while a uniform response everywhere is harder to defend. The test is designed to be able to fail.

questions.explanation: A recovery that would have happened anyway looks identical to one caused by the work unless a counterfactual is built. The comparison designs are what separate the two, and a test that cannot fail proves nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what would have happened without the intervention.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Detect a causal claim that reaches forward in time

stimulus.body: In 1994 the wetland was drained and a heron roost site was fenced. Thirty years later the heron population has recovered to more than the pre-drainage count, and the management note attributes the recovery entirely to the fencing. A paragraph in the same note records that the fencing was removed in 2003 and replaced with a bund of a different design.

questions.stem: Given this note, how much of the recovery can the fencing claim carry?

options.text: The recovery proves the fencing worked, because herons are now above the old count
options.misconception: credits the earlier measure while ignoring a later one

options.text: The recovery cannot be credited to the fencing alone, since the design changed later
The herons returned because wetlands drain slowly and nothing human mattered
options.misconception: removes human action entirely from a managed site

options.text: The bund was a failure, since the herons did not arrive until the fences came down
options.misconception: treats the later date as proof that the later measure failed

questions.explanation: The note itself records that the protective measure was replaced, so the surviving herons cannot be attributed to the original fencing without more evidence. Reading the end of the story back onto the first intervention is hindsight inside a causal claim.
questions.hint: Ask which measure was in place when the recovery came.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Order explanations that operate at different scales
questions.stem: A survey team must explain why a beetle population collapsed on one managed grassland; which framing best handles the scale of the question?

options.text: Field conditions explain the loss, while the national policy set the conditions
National policy caused the loss, and the field record is only a local detail
options.misconception: lets the largest scale swallow the others

options.text: Field conditions caused the loss, and nothing at national scale needs examining
options.misconception: confines causation to the scale closest to the data

options.text: No scale is appropriate, since the two levels cannot be compared at all
options.misconception: declines to compare scales instead of ordering them

questions.explanation: Explanations at different scales answer different parts of the same question, and a policy-level account and a field-level account can be compatible. The alternatives either promote one scale into the whole story or refuse to relate them.
questions.hint: Ask which level each piece of evidence speaks to.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish presence of a factor from weight of evidence
questions.stem: A grassland restoration is credited with equal weight to a fencing change and a twenty-year shift in rainfall, because both were said to matter.

options.text: Equal weighting is fair, because both factors were present during the period
options.misconception: treats presence in the period as equal causal weight

options.text: The rainfall should count for more, since weather always dominates biology
options.misconception: reasons from a general expectation instead of the local record

options.text: The fence should count for more, since human actions are usually decisive
options.misconception: assumes human agency outranks environment by default

options.text: The record may support one factor carrying far more of the effect

questions.explanation: Weighting contributors requires comparing how much of the outcome each can account for, not counting the factors. Where one factor was absent in comparable situations that showed no decline, it may reasonably carry more weight.
questions.hint: Ask which factor was absent where the effect did not occur.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Choose between accounts that both fit one observation
questions.stem: A survey attributes a gull colony's move from one cliff to a new food source, while a second survey attributes the same move to a predator's arrival on the old cliff.

options.text: The food explanation is better, because colonies always follow the best food source
options.misconception: prefers a general rule over the specific evidence

options.text: The predator explanation is better, because predators usually drive colony moves
options.misconception: reasons from a general expectation rather than the local record

options.text: The surveys must weigh dates, distances and the absence of alternative drivers
Both explanations are equally good, so the choice between them is a matter of taste
options.misconception: mistakes an unresolved choice for an equal one

questions.explanation: When two accounts fit the same observation, the choice must be made on what each account predicts about timing, magnitude and the presence of alternatives. Equal fit to one observation is not a reason to stop thinking.
questions.hint: Ask what each account predicts about dates and distance.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Test a causal claim whose effect precedes the cause
questions.stem: In a coastal survey, the numbers of shell fragments on the beach fall three years before the harbour wall extension that the report calls the cause.

options.text: The wall extension caused the fall, since the wall is clearly the later structure
options.misconception: credits the later structure because it is the more visible one

options.text: The fall predates the wall, so the wall cannot explain the earliest decline
The fall was caused by the wall, since the wall will slow the waves further
options.misconception: credits a cause on the strength of its future effect

options.text: Shell counts cannot be used to date changes at all
options.misconception: dismisses a dated record rather than reading it

questions.explanation: A cause that arrives three years after the effect began cannot account for that beginning, whatever it does later. The record therefore points to an earlier driver, and the wall would need a separate argument.
questions.hint: Ask which came first in the shell counts.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A chain rather than a single cause
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a linked sequence carries an outcome
questions.stem: Explain to a management group how a sequence of linked changes can carry an outcome that no single change could.

answer.exemplar: A chain explains an outcome by naming a sequence in which each link makes the next more likely, so that removing any one link weakens the whole. If a drain is deepened, then the reed bed dries, then the vole population falls, then the harrier abandons the site, then the wader chicks fail, then no overall loss occurs and the reed bed recovers, so each link is necessary for the final effect. The chain also shows where intervention is most efficient, since breaking the cheapest link is usually cheaper than repairing the whole sequence. A single-cause account has to stretch to cover all of these steps.

questions.explanation: Outcomes that no one change can produce are usually explained by chains, and each link in the chain is a candidate point of leverage. Naming a single cause for such an outcome forces the account to skip the steps that carried it.
questions.hint: Ask which step in the sequence makes the next one possible.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish evidence of visibility from evidence of recovery

stimulus.body: The reserve's management report describes the reintroduction of the species as a success and notes that visitor numbers at the hide have risen sharply since the release year. The report gives no post-release population counts, and the only monitoring figure listed is the number of hide tickets sold. The board is asked to record the reintroduction as a proven recovery.

questions.stem: Given this report, what does the evidence actually establish?

options.text: The hide tickets show the species is breeding, since visitors came to see it
options.misconception: reads visitor interest as evidence of breeding

options.text: The record shows visibility of the species but not the recovery that was claimed
Rising visitor numbers prove the recovery, because people want to see what returned
options.misconception: treats public interest as a proxy for population change

options.text: Without a breeding count the reintroduction cannot be judged at all
options.misconception: denies that partial evidence supports any judgement

questions.explanation: Visitor numbers measure interest in the species, not its population size, so the report's evidence does not reach the recovery it claims. Progress in a reintroduction needs population or reproduction data measured over time.
questions.hint: Ask what the ticket numbers actually measure.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State the status of a period boundary accurately
questions.stem: A regional history divides its chapters by administrative reform; which statement best reflects the status of that division?

options.text: The division is a defensible choice if the records support what changed after it
The division is true because each period is a named stretch of calendar time
options.misconception: treats a named stretch of time as self-justifying

options.text: Periods should follow the length of the source material they describe
options.misconception: lets the evidence base dictate the period rather than vice versa

options.text: Any division is arbitrary, so the history should use one undifferentiated span
options.misconception: concludes that all periodization is invalid because some is chosen

questions.explanation: Periodization is always a choice, and the question is whether the chosen boundaries illuminate something the sources show. Dividing by administrative reform is legitimate when reform actually reorganised the record.
questions.hint: Ask what changed after the boundary the author chose.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Require local confirmation of a candidate common driver
questions.stem: A rodent survey finds the same decline in two distant catchments, and the report blames the introduction of a farming practice in each.

options.text: The same practice explains both declines, since the outcome is identical
options.misconception: assumes matching effects must have matching causes

options.text: Only the catchments with more agriculture can be affected by a farming practice
options.misconception: restricts a causal claim to the cases that fit it best

options.text: The declines must be unrelated, since the two catchments share no individuals
options.misconception: treats spatial separation as proof of separate causes

options.text: The shared practice is a candidate driver that each catchment still needs testing

questions.explanation: A common practice across two catchments makes it a serious candidate, but the local records still have to be checked for other drivers. Treating a shared explanation as proven ignores what else may have changed at each site.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a comparison that tests whether a treatment mattered
questions.stem: A team claims a fence saved a colony of ground-nesting birds and notes that colonies in unfenced fields nearby did not recover.

options.text: The fence worked, because the nearby colonies are known to be weaker stock
options.misconception: assumes a difference in the populations that was never checked

options.text: The fence cannot be tested, because neighbouring fields always behave differently
options.misconception: dismisses a comparison because sites are never identical

options.text: The nearby colonies give a comparison in which the fence was absent
The fence is irrelevant, since birds move between fenced and unfenced fields
options.misconception: removes the comparison by assuming movement between sites

questions.explanation: A neighbouring site without the intervention is exactly the comparison a contingency test needs, because it shows what happened where the intervention was absent. The alternatives either invent differences or dissolve the comparison by assumption.
questions.hint: Ask what happened where the fence was absent.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Detect a later measure invoked to explain an earlier outcome
questions.stem: A fisheries report explains a 1970s collapse of the cod stock by naming a modern stock rebuilding rule.

options.text: The modern rule explains the collapse, since it governs the same stock
options.misconception: applies a later rule to an earlier collapse

options.text: The collapse and the rule belong to different periods and cannot be linked that way
The collapse proves that every later rule was unnecessary
options.misconception: reads a past failure as a verdict on later measures

options.text: The rule was written because of the collapse, so the link is a direct cause
options.misconception: reverses the direction of a retrospective rule

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an account must declare the scale it operates at
questions.stem: Explain to a survey team why an explanation should name the scale at which it operates.

answer.exemplar: An explanation at one scale leaves out the variables that operate at another, so naming the scale shows what the account can and cannot cover. A field-level account of a vegetation change names rainfall, grazing and soil, and can be tested against plots in the same region. A regional-level account names the policy or land-use regime that set those local conditions across a wide area. Saying which level is meant stops a local pattern being presented as a national cause, and stops a national claim being refuted by one awkward field.

questions.explanation: Claims fail when a level of explanation is presented as though it were another. Declaring the scale tells a reader what the account addresses and what remains outside it.
questions.hint: Ask which level the evidence and the claim both belong to.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the comparison needed to weigh contributing factors

stimulus.body: An upland moor restoration reduced sheep numbers by 40 percent, restored a blanket of sphagnum, and coincided with three wetter summers. The evaluation credits the fencing and the reduced stocking with the whole improvement, and treats the wetter summers as a fortunate backdrop that did not matter. A neighbouring moor with no fence and no reduction in stocking is not reported.

questions.stem: Given this evaluation, what is missing before the contributors can be weighed?

options.text: The wetter summers must have produced the sphagnum recovery
options.misconception: credits weather without showing a comparison site

options.text: The fencing produced the recovery, since stocking changes take decades to work
options.misconception: reasons from a general timescale rather than the record

options.text: The improved moor shows what reduced stocking alone would have achieved
options.misconception: credits a treatment that was never applied on its own

options.text: The unreported neighbouring moor is the comparison needed to weigh the factors

questions.explanation: Without a similar moor that received neither treatment, the evaluation cannot separate the effect of reduced stocking from three wetter summers. The missing comparison is exactly what would let the contributors be weighed against each other.
questions.hint: Ask what happened on a moor that received no treatment.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Separate two accounts that both fit the same observation
questions.stem: Two accounts of a fish die-off, one blaming a heat event and one blaming a chemical discharge, fit the timing equally well; which step should come next?

options.text: Compare what each account predicts for other years and other sites
Choose the account with the more familiar cause, since familiarity aids judgement
options.misconception: prefers the familiar explanation over the better supported one

options.text: Average the two accounts, since the truth about a die-off is always partial
options.misconception: mistakes a compromise for a settled explanation

options.text: Keep both accounts, since choosing one of them is unnecessary work
options.misconception: treats an unresolved question as a finished one

questions.explanation: Two accounts that fit one observation equally must be separated by what they predict elsewhere. Extrapolating each to other years and sites is the cheapest way to see which survives contact with more data.
questions.hint: Ask what each account predicts for other years and sites.

questions.learningObjective: Show that a proposed cause arrives after its effect
questions.stem: A river survey records the loss of gravel spawning beds three years before the abstraction licence that the report treats as the cause.

options.misconception: credits a cause from a general principle alone

options.misconception: treats rarity as a bar on all causal reasoning

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how hindsight enters and can be guarded against
questions.stem: Explain to a monitoring team how hindsight can enter a causal claim and how to guard against it.

answer.exemplar: Hindsight enters when knowledge of the outcome is used to select the cause, so the explanation is fitted to a result that was already known. A team that sees a marsh fail after a wet year may name the wet year and then look for support in the same record. The guard is to fix the candidate causes before the outcome is known, to write down what each candidate predicts, and to check the record for a period with the cause present and the outcome absent. Causes that only look plausible because the outcome is known are thereby excluded.

questions.explanation: Explaining a known outcome from known causes lets the outcome select its own explanation. Fixing the candidate list in advance and checking for the cause's presence without the effect is the practical safeguard.
questions.hint: Ask which causes were listed before the result was known.

options.misconception: treats a scale mismatch as a reason to refuse the assessment

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A chain rather than a single cause
questions.learningObjective: Explain why several pressures in sequence form a chain
questions.stem: Explain to a fisheries group why a collapse with several contributing pressures is often best described as a chain.

answer.exemplar: A chain is the right description when the pressures acted in sequence, each making the next more damaging, so that the final collapse required all of them. If warming reduced prey, small fish grew slower, seabird numbers fell, and the remaining fishery took more stock to catch, then no single pressure explains the outcome and none of them was fatal on its own. A chain description also gives the group an ordering of interventions, since relieving the slowest link may matter more than removing the most visible one. Single-cause accounts of such collapses usually describe one link and drop the rest.

questions.explanation: When several pressures act in sequence and none is sufficient alone, the chain is what the evidence supports. Single-cause accounts of such collapses usually describe one link and leave the rest out.
questions.hint: Ask which pressure made the next one more damaging.

options.misconception: credits a general known cause instead of weighing the local record

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to break a tie between two fitting accounts
questions.stem: Explain to a review panel how to choose between two explanations that both fit the same observation.

answer.exemplar: When two accounts fit one observation, the choice has to rest on what each predicts beyond that observation. A good test is to write down, before looking further, what each account would predict for another year, another site or another measure, and then to look for a place where the predictions differ. The account that survives at least one such test, and that accounts for the size as well as the timing, is the better supported of the two. Writing the predictions down first stops the team from adjusting an account after every observation.

questions.explanation: Two accounts that fit the same observation are not equally good simply because they both fit. Extrapolating each to a case where they disagree turns a tie into a decision.
questions.hint: Ask where the two accounts would predict different results.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how scale determines what counts as evidence
questions.stem: Explain to a funding body how the scale of an explanation changes what counts as evidence for it.

answer.exemplar: The scale of a claim sets the observations that could confirm or refute it. A claim that a national policy caused a regional decline predicts that declines appear wherever the policy applied and not where it did not, so regional and national records are both relevant. A claim that a local groundworks caused the same decline predicts a change at that site and no comparable change nearby, so a distant policy record is neither support nor refutation. Writing the scale down at the start tells the team which comparisons to gather, instead of collecting data that happens to be available.

questions.explanation: Evidence that speaks to one scale is silent at another, and gathering the wrong evidence wastes a survey season. Declaring the scale first fixes what a fair test would look like.
questions.hint: Ask what observations could have refuted the claim.

questions.explanation: A justification written after the outcome was known is not evidence, however accurate it later turns out to be. The plan may still be good, but its stated grounds rest on knowledge unavailable at the time.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a shared driver needs separate local testing
questions.stem: Explain to a regional office why a driver operating in two regions must be tested in each region separately.

answer.exemplar: A driver that appears in both regions is a candidate common cause, but each region can carry it into a different outcome because the local conditions differ. The same herbicide may reduce insects in a farmland catchment and simply coincide with a decline in a peatland where it is hardly used, because something else dominates there. Testing the driver in each region means checking that it operated, that its timing matches, and that the outcome followed where it did. A driver confirmed in one region and assumed in another has been evidenced in only one place.

questions.explanation: Shared drivers still need local confirmation, because the same input can act through very different local conditions. Carrying a result across regions without checking transfers an assumption rather than a finding.
questions.hint: Ask whether the driver actually operated in each region.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how unequal weights between contributing factors are judged
questions.stem: Explain to a station manager how unequal weights between contributing factors should be judged.

answer.exemplar: Judging weights means asking how much of the outcome each factor can account for, using evidence such as presence, absence and dose rather than the order in which factors are listed. A factor that was absent where the outcome also did not occur carries more weight than one that was present in both cases. Where several factors operated together, a study that varied one of them holds the others steady and gives the best estimate of its share. Factors named because they are familiar or visible often carry weight in the writing that the evidence does not support, and that mismatch is the error to guard against.

questions.explanation: Weighting is a matter of how much each factor explains, not of how prominent it is in the account. Estimating shares requires variation, and factors named for visibility or familiarity get credit that the evidence has not earned.
questions.hint: Ask how much of the outcome each factor can explain.

options.misconception: prefers contemporary opinion over later evidence without argument

options.text: The account may be right, but its grounds are later knowledge rather than proof

questions.explanation: Later writers can add evidence that earlier ones lacked, but a claim justified only by hindsight has not been shown to follow from the record available at the time. The distinction matters when assessing what an earlier decision could have been based on.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence was available when the outcome happened.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Assess a local cause named in a broad report
questions.stem: A national survey attributes a decline in one coastal fishery to a local dredging scheme, and the national report offers no detail of the fishery.

options.text: The national attribution is strong, since it rests on the wider dataset
options.misconception: mistakes scale of evidence for strength of explanation

options.text: The local scheme is a candidate cause that needs local evidence
The national attribution must be wrong, since it lacks local detail
options.misconception: rejects a claim for missing detail that the claim never needed

options.text: The scheme is irrelevant, since dredging has never affected a fishery
options.misconception: denies a plausible mechanism because it is unfamiliar

questions.explanation: A national account that names a local cause must show the link in the places affected, and the report offers none. The local scheme remains a candidate that the local record could confirm or rule out.
questions.hint: Ask what local evidence the attribution rests on.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A chain rather than a single cause
questions.learningObjective: Read a sequence of dated changes as a linked chain
questions.stem: In a coastal catchment, quail eggs fall 15 percent after a 20 percent loss of salt marsh, and in the following year a 30 percent rise in the number of rats follows the egg fall.

options.text: The marsh loss caused the quail decline, and the rats are a separate effect
options.misconception: cuts a linked sequence at the first measurable step

options.text: The rat rise caused the marsh loss, since predators thin reed beds
options.misconception: reverses a sequence that the dates themselves contradict

options.text: The marsh loss, the egg fall and the rat rise form a linked sequence
None of the three steps matters, since quail numbers fluctuate every year
options.misconception: uses ordinary fluctuation to dismiss a documented sequence

questions.explanation: The dates and sizes fit a sequence in which each step makes the next more likely, and the second step depends on the first being understood. Reading only the first pair of numbers truncates the explanation the record supports.
questions.hint: Ask what each step made more likely than the one before.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a chosen period boundary must be argued for
questions.stem: Explain to a district office why periodization is a choice that has to be defended.

answer.exemplar: Every period boundary is chosen, so the question is never whether the author chose one but whether the choice shows something the record reveals. A survey history that begins a period at a change in the substrate, the drainage or the settlement pattern is claiming that this is where the earlier phase ends and the next begins. To defend it, the author can point to what the records show changing at that date, and to the fact that observations before and after it are not directly comparable. Boundaries that reflect the archive's own conventions can be useful, provided they are declared rather than smuggled in.

questions.explanation: Periodization is a claim about where one phase ends and another begins, and the claim needs evidence behind it. Undeclared boundaries let the archive's convenience pass as the shape of the past.
questions.hint: Ask what the records show changing at the boundary.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Weaken a broad cause using a neighbouring comparison

stimulus.body: A field review of a catchment concludes that fish numbers fell because of a change in the law governing net fishing in the region in 1996. The review's data come from the catchment's own sampling programme. Elsewhere in the same document, the author notes that the neighbouring catchment, which was outside the 1996 law for its first five years and inside it afterwards, recorded no comparable fall in its fish.

questions.stem: Given this review, what does the neighbouring catchment do to the argument?

options.text: The legal explanation is sound, because it applies to every fishery in the region
options.misconception: assumes a rule applies with equal effect everywhere it applies

options.text: The neighbouring catchment weakens the legal explanation and needs accounting for
The review is right, because the law is the only change the data can detect
options.misconception: treats detectability as evidence of causation

options.text: The review is wrong, because the neighbouring catchment must have been surveyed differently
options.misconception: asserts a methodological difference the document does not mention

questions.explanation: A cause that operated in one catchment and not the other, with no matching difference in outcome, is weakened by the comparison. The review must either explain the neighbouring record or narrow its claim.
questions.hint: Ask why the neighbouring catchment did not fall.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State what a contingency claim still requires to be shown
questions.stem: A second grazing trial reports that excluding stock from a hill doubled the orchids; which statement best expresses what would still need showing?

options.text: That the orchids would have doubled without the exclusion as well
options.misconception: asks for a comparison that would dissolve the treatment effect

options.text: That the hill is large enough for the result to matter to the population
options.misconception: shifts the question from causation to practical importance

options.text: That no other hill in the district received the same treatment
options.misconception: asks about treatment spread rather than the effect of treatment

options.text: That the doubling would not have happened on comparable grazed ground

questions.explanation: Contingency is a claim about what would have happened otherwise, so it needs a case where the exclusion was absent and the orchids did not double. Scale and spread matter for other reasons, but they do not test the causal claim.
questions.hint: Ask what comparable grazed ground would have shown.
